summary.text: Define the candidate linear-recurrence sequence \(L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\) and the defect \(f_n=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n\); induction from \(f_{n+3}=4f_{n+1}+f_n\), together with growth and positivity of \(L\), proves \(0<f_n\le L_n\). Thus \(L_{n+1}^2=L_{n+2}L_n+f_n\) has a positive remainder no larger than the denominator, so the ceiling-minus-one rule returns exactly \(L_{n+2}\), and induction identifies the originally defined sequence with the linear recurrence underlying the claimed generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(m\ge 0\),
\[
b_{m+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{m+1}^2}{b_m}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{1}
\]
For positive terms, this is exactly the formulation saying that \(b_{m+2}\) is the greatest integer satisfying
\[
\frac{b_{m+2}}{b_{m+1}}<\frac{b_{m+1}}{b_m},
\]
because this strict inequality is equivalent to
\(b_{m+2}<b_{m+1}^2/b_m\), and the greatest integer strictly less than a real number \(y\) is \(\lceil y\rceil-1\).

We prove that \((b_n)\) satisfies
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\]
and
\[
b_{m+3}=4b_{m+2}-b_m\qquad(m\ge 0).
\tag{2}
\]
This recurrence will then immediately give the claimed generating function.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((L_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
L_0=4,\qquad L_1=16,\qquad L_2=63,
\]
and
\[
L_{m+3}=4L_{m+2}-L_m\qquad(m\ge0).
\tag{3}
\]
The main task is to prove that the nonlinear sequence \(b_n\) agrees with \(L_n\).

First we record positivity and monotonicity of \(L_n\):
\[
1\le L_n<L_{n+1}\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{4}
\]
The first few terms are
\[
L_0=4,
\quad L_1=16,
\quad L_2=63,
\quad L_3=4\cdot63-4=248,
\]
so (4) holds initially. Suppose inductively that the needed inequalities hold at all earlier indices. For an index of the form \(m+3\), the preceding inequalities give
\[
0<L_{m+1}<L_{m+2}<L_{m+3}.
\]
Using (3) one index later,
\[
L_{m+4}=4L_{m+3}-L_{m+1}.
\]
Since \(L_{m+1}<L_{m+3}\) and \(L_{m+3}>0\), we have
\[
L_{m+4}>3L_{m+3}>L_{m+3}.
\]
This proves the induction step and hence (4). In particular, every \(L_n\) is positive.

We will also need the growth estimate
\[
4L_{m+1}+2L_m\le 4L_{m+2}
\qquad(m\ge0).
\tag{5}
\]
For \(m=0\), it reads
\[
4\cdot16+2\cdot4=72\le252=4\cdot63.
\]
Now let \(m=p+1\). By (3),
\[
L_{p+3}=4L_{p+2}-L_p.
\]
Thus (5) at \(m=p+1\) is equivalent to
\[
4L_{p+2}+2L_{p+1}\le16L_{p+2}-4L_p,
\]
or
\[
2L_{p+1}+4L_p\le12L_{p+2}.
\]
This follows at once from positivity and
\(L_p<L_{p+1}<L_{p+2}\): indeed, the left side is strictly less than
\(6L_{p+2}\), which is at most \(12L_{p+2}\). Therefore (5) holds for every \(m\).

Next define the defect
\[
f_k=L_{k+1}^2-L_{k+2}L_k.
\tag{6}
\]
The crucial assertion is
\[
0<f_k\le L_k\qquad(k\ge0).
\tag{7}
\]

We first derive a recurrence for the defects:
\[
f_{m+3}=4f_{m+1}+f_m.
\tag{8}
\]
For completeness, write
\[
A=L_m,\quad B=L_{m+1},\quad C=L_{m+2},
\]
so that, by (3),
\[
D:=L_{m+3}=4C-A,
\quad E:=L_{m+4}=4D-B,
\quad L_{m+5}=4E-C.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{m+3}
 &=E^2-(4E-C)D\\
 &=E(E-4D)+CD\\
 &=-BE+CD\\
 &=-B(4D-B)+CD\\
 &=B^2+D(C-4B).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting \(D=4C-A\) and expanding gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{m+3}
 &=B^2+(4C-A)(C-4B)\\
 &=4(C^2-DB)+(B^2-CA)\\
 &=4f_{m+1}+f_m,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (8).

The three initial defects are
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_0&=L_1^2-L_2L_0=16^2-63\cdot4=4,\\
f_1&=L_2^2-L_3L_1=63^2-248\cdot16=1,\\
f_2&=L_3^2-L_4L_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here
\[
L_4=4L_3-L_1=4\cdot248-16=976,
\]
so
\[
f_2=248^2-976\cdot63=16.
\]
Consequently
\[
0<f_0=4\le L_0=4,
\quad 0<f_1=1\le L_1=16,
\quad 0<f_2=16\le L_2=63.
\]

Assume inductively that (7) holds at all indices below \(m+3\). In particular,
\[
0<f_m\le L_m,
\qquad
0<f_{m+1}\le L_{m+1}.
\]
Equation (8) immediately gives \(f_{m+3}>0\). For the upper bound, it gives
\[
f_{m+3}=4f_{m+1}+f_m
 \le4L_{m+1}+L_m.
\]
By the growth estimate (5),
\[
4L_{m+1}+2L_m\le4L_{m+2},
\]
and hence
\[
4L_{m+1}+L_m\le4L_{m+2}-L_m=L_{m+3},
\]
where the last equality is (3). Thus
\(f_{m+3}\le L_{m+3}\), completing the induction and proving (7).

We now show by strong induction that
\[
b_n=L_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{9}
\]
This is immediate for \(n=0,1\). Suppose that the equality has already been proved through indices \(m+1\). By (6),
\[
L_{m+1}^2=L_{m+2}L_m+f_m.
\tag{10}
\]
By (7),
\[
1\le f_m\le L_m,
\tag{11}
\]
and by (4), \(L_m>0\).

Using the induction hypothesis \(b_m=L_m\) and \(b_{m+1}=L_{m+1}\), equations (10) and (11) say that
\[
b_{m+1}^2=L_{m+2}b_m+f_m,
\qquad 1\le f_m\le b_m.
\tag{12}
\]
We claim that (12) forces the ceiling expression in (1) to be exactly \(L_{m+2}\). This is the elementary division fact behind the proof. In general, if \(d>0\) and
\[
N=qd+r,\qquad 1\le r\le d,
\]
then
\[
q<\frac Nd\le q+1.
\]
Therefore \(\lceil N/d\rceil=q+1\), and so
\[
\left\lceil\frac Nd\right\rceil-1=q.
\tag{13}
\]
Applying (13) to
\[
N=b_{m+1}^2,
\quad d=b_m,
\quad q=L_{m+2},
\quad r=f_m,
\]
and using (12), we obtain
\[
b_{m+2}
 =\left\lceil\frac{b_{m+1}^2}{b_m}\right\rceil-1
 =L_{m+2}.
\]
This proves the induction step, hence (9) for every \(n\). It also proves along the way that all terms of the originally defined sequence are positive, justifying the ratio formulation of its definition.

Since \(b_n=L_n\), the defining recurrence (3) for \(L_n\) transfers to \(b_n\):
\[
b_{m+3}=4b_{m+2}-b_m\qquad(m\ge0).
\]
The right side is positive, so this equality is equally valid whether regarded as an equality of integers or of nonnegative integers. Also
\[
b_2=L_2=63.
\]
Thus, in the indexing used in the conjecture,
\[
b_n=
\begin{cases}
4,&n=0,\\
16,&n=1,\\
63,&n=2,\\
4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3},&n\ge3.
\end{cases}
\tag{14}
\]

Finally let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, interpreted as a formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^0\) in
\((1-4x+x^3)G(x)\) is \(b_0=4\). The coefficient of \(x^1\) is
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0,
\]
and the coefficient of \(x^2\) is
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
For every \(n\ge3\), the coefficient is
\[
b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3}=0
\]
by (14). Consequently
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)=4-x^2,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
This proves the conjectured generating function for the sequence defined by the original consecutive-ratio rule.
